name: Titanium Dioxide
euDetails: Banned across the European Union for all food uses under Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/63. EFSA safety evaluation concluded it can no longer be considered safe due to genotoxicity concerns and accumulation of nanoparticles.
fssaiDetails: Permitted by FSSAI under Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations up to 10,000 mg/kg (1%) in chewing gums, sweets, and powdered drink mixes.
fssaiCitation: FSS (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations 2011, Appendix A
fdaDetails: Permitted as a color additive exempt from certification up to 1% by weight of food under 21 CFR 73.575.
explanation: Titanium dioxide is an inorganic whitening pigment banned in Europe due to DNA damage (genotoxicity) risks, yet widely used in Indian confectionery, cake decor, and powdered drink premixes.

name: Tartrazine
euDetails: Subject to mandatory statutory warning label in the EU: 'may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children' under Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 Annex V. Many European manufacturers have voluntarily phased it out in favor of turmeric/beta-carotene.
fssaiDetails: Permitted synthetic food color under FSSAI regulations up to 100 mg/kg (or 200 mg/kg in canned foods) with no mandatory child hyperactivity warning required.
fssaiCitation: FSS (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations & Food Additives Compendium
fdaDetails: Permitted subject to batch certification (FD&C Yellow No. 5). Mandatory declaration on ingredient labels due to documented allergic and asthmatic reactions.
explanation: One of the six 'Southampton Six' azo dyes linked to hyperactivity and ADHD symptoms in children. Requires explicit warning in the EU, while permitted in India without any child warning.

name: Sunset Yellow FCF
euDetails: Mandatory EU warning required under Annex V: 'may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children'. EFSA lowered the ADI to 1 mg/kg bw in 2014.
fssaiDetails: Permitted synthetic food color under FSSAI up to 100 mg/kg without child warning requirements. Widely found in orange sodas, namkeens, and sweets in India.
fssaiCitation: FSS (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations 2011
fdaDetails: Permitted certified color (FD&C Yellow No. 6) under 21 CFR 74.706.
explanation: Southampton dye linked to child behavioral issues and allergic responses. EU products formulate with paprika or carrot extract instead; Indian formulations frequently rely on synthetic INS 110.

name: Carmoisine (Azorubine)
euDetails: Requires mandatory Annex V child hyperactivity warning: 'may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children'.
fssaiDetails: Permitted synthetic red color in specified food matrices up to 100 mg/kg.
fdaDetails: Not approved as a food color additive in the United States by the FDA.
explanation: Red azo dye unapproved in the US and restricted in the EU with child hyperactivity warnings, but commonly used in Indian jams, ice creams, and syrups.

name: Ponceau 4R
euDetails: Subject to mandatory Annex V warning: 'may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children'.
fssaiDetails: Permitted in India in specified products up to 100 mg/kg without behavioral warnings.
fdaDetails: Not authorized by the FDA for use in foods in the United States.
explanation: Synthetic strawberry-red color banned in the US and warning-mandated in Europe, but standard in Indian confectionery and fruit-flavored beverages.

name: Allura Red AC
euDetails: Requires mandatory child warning under Annex V: 'may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children'.
fssaiDetails: Permitted synthetic color up to 100 mg/kg under FSSAI regulations.
fdaDetails: Permitted certified color (FD&C Red No. 40) under 21 CFR 74.340.
explanation: Widely used red colorant requiring warning in the EU due to behavioral concerns in young children.

name: Quinoline Yellow
euDetails: Authorized in the EU but subject to Annex V child warning: 'may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children'.
fssaiDetails: Not permitted in the general synthetic food color list for most standard food categories in India under FSSAI.
fdaDetails: Not permitted in foods by US FDA.
explanation: A dye not permitted under FSSAI's primary authorized food color list, showing regulatory strictness in India for certain synthetic dyes.

name: Erythrosine
euDetails: Severely restricted in the EU: authorized ONLY for cocktail cherries, candied cherries, and Bigarreaux cherries (max 150-200 mg/kg). Prohibited in all other foods.
fssaiDetails: Permitted in India in designated foods up to 100 mg/kg.
fdaDetails: Banned by US FDA for cosmetics and externally applied drugs in 1990 due to animal thyroid cancer evidence. Banned in food by California Food Safety Act (AB 418, effective 2027); under active federal FDA review.
explanation: Organoiodine red dye associated with thyroid disruption and carcinogenicity in animal models. Heavily restricted in Europe, while allowed in India.

name: Brominated Vegetable Oil
euDetails: Never authorized as a food additive in the EU (not on positive list under Regulation (EC) 1333/2008).
fssaiDetails: Prohibited in India under FSS (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations.
fssaiCitation: FSS (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations 2011
fdaDetails: FDA revoked its regulation authorizing the use of BVO in food in July 2024 (21 CFR 180.30) due to bioaccumulation of bromine in body tissues and thyroid toxicity.
explanation: Historical clouding agent in citrus sodas now banned across US, EU, and India due to organ damage and bromine accumulation.

name: Potassium Bromate
euDetails: Banned in the European Union in 1990 due to IARC classification as Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans).
fssaiDetails: Banned by FSSAI in 2016 from all bakery products following a study by the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) revealing cancer risks.
fdaDetails: Permitted in bread flour up to 75 ppm under 21 CFR 136.110, though FDA has urged bakers to voluntarily cease its use.
explanation: A powerful flour improver that FSSAI proactively banned in India in 2016, following the EU's lead, despite US FDA still permitting it.

name: Shellac
euDetails: Authorized glazing agent under Regulation (EC) 1333/2008 Annex II.
fssaiDetails: Permitted glazing agent. Crucially, under FSSAI Labelling regulations, food additives of insect origin are legally exempt from triggering the brown non-vegetarian logo, so products with Shellac frequently carry India's Green Veg Dot.
fdaDetails: Permitted as GRAS for confectionery glaze.
explanation: Derived from the secretion of female lac insects (Kerria lacca). Millions of strict vegetarians and vegans in India consume it unknowingly because FSSAI regulations do not classify insect glazes as non-vegetarian.

name: Beeswax (White & Yellow)
euDetails: Authorized glazing agent under Regulation (EC) 1333/2008.
fssaiDetails: Permitted glazing agent. Exempt from India's mandatory brown non-veg dot despite being a honeybee byproduct.
fdaDetails: GRAS under 21 CFR 184.1973.
explanation: Harvested from honeybee combs. Carries the green vegetarian dot on Indian snacks and sweets despite being animal-derived, creating a transparency blindspot for strict vegans.

name: L-Cysteine
euDetails: Permitted in flour treatment. In 2012, EU explicitly prohibited using human hair as a raw material source (Directive 2010/69/EU).
fssaiDetails: Permitted in bakery products up to 90 mg/kg. Does not mandate declaring the biological source (duck feathers vs. microbial), and packages routinely carry the Green Veg Dot.
fssaiCitation: FSS (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations 2011
fdaDetails: GRAS under 21 CFR 184.1271.
explanation: Often sourced industrially from poultry feathers (or pig bristles). Under Indian labelling laws, processing aids and micro-additives do not require a brown non-veg dot, masking its animal origin.

name: Carmine / Cochineal
euDetails: Authorized red color under Regulation (EC) 1333/2008. Must be declared as 'carmine' or 'cochineal' due to severe allergen potential.
fssaiDetails: Permitted natural color. In India, cochineal is derived from crushed female insects, which contradicts traditional vegetarian dietary practices.
fdaDetails: Must be explicitly declared on food labels by name ('carmine' or 'cochineal extract') to alert allergic individuals (21 CFR 73.100).
explanation: Extracted from crushed female cochineal insects. While natural, it is unsuitable for vegetarians and vegans.

name: Palmolein / Refined Palm Oil
euDetails: Permitted, but EU Regulation 1169/2011 mandates specific vegetable oil declaration (cannot just hide behind 'Vegetable Oil'). EFSA monitors 3-MCPD and glycidyl esters in refined palm oil for nephrotoxicity and genotoxic carcinogenicity.
fssaiDetails: Standard frying oil used across 90%+ of packaged Indian chips, namkeens, and biscuits due to low cost and long shelf life.
fdaDetails: Permitted conventional food fat.
explanation: High in saturated palmitic acid (approx. 50%) and industrial processing contaminants. While European snack makers predominantly reformulate with high-oleic sunflower or rapeseed oil, Indian packaged foods almost universally rely on palmolein.

name: Monosodium Glutamate (MSG)
euDetails: Authorized in the EU with a group maximum limit of 10 g/kg (as glutamic acid).
fssaiDetails: Permitted under GMP in specified foods. Must carry 'Not recommended for infants below 12 months' on retail packaging.
fdaDetails: Recognized as GRAS by FDA.
explanation: Classic industrial flavor enhancer indicating high palatability engineering and ultra-processing (NOVA-4).

name: Disodium Guanylate
euDetails: Authorized food additive in EU under Regulation 1333/2008.
fssaiDetails: Permitted under GMP in snack foods and seasonings.
fdaDetails: Permitted flavor enhancer under 21 CFR 172.530.
explanation: Synergistic flavor enhancer typically paired with MSG or inosinate in ultra-processed chips, noodles, and savory seasonings.

name: Disodium Inosinate
euDetails: Authorized additive in EU.
fssaiDetails: Permitted under GMP in processed foods.
fdaDetails: Permitted flavor enhancer under 21 CFR 172.535.
explanation: Flavor enhancer derived from yeast or meat/fish extracts, frequently used to amplify savory taste in ultra-processed snacks.

name: Disodium 5'-Ribonucleotides
euDetails: Authorized in EU.
fssaiDetails: Permitted under GMP in instant noodles and seasonings.
fdaDetails: Approved food additive.
explanation: Equimolar mixture of disodium inosinate and disodium guanylate, characteristic of industrial noodle tastemakers and potato crisps.

name: Acesulfame Potassium (Ace-K)
euDetails: Authorized with strict maximum usable levels per food category. WHO guideline advises against non-sugar sweeteners for body weight control.
fssaiDetails: Permitted in designated foods with statutory declaration: 'Contains Artificial Sweetener'.
fdaDetails: Approved general-purpose sweetener under 21 CFR 172.800.
explanation: Zero-calorie synthetic sweetener ~200 times sweeter than sucrose. Indicator of ultra-processed diet beverages and confectioneries.

name: Aspartame
euDetails: Authorized in the EU. Mandatory label statement: 'contains a source of phenylalanine' for phenylketonuria sufferers. IARC classified aspartame as Group 2B (possibly carcinogenic to humans) in 2023.
fssaiDetails: Permitted with mandatory warning: 'Contains Aspartame. Not recommended for children.' and 'Phenylketonurics: Contains Phenylalanine'.
fdaDetails: Permitted with mandatory Phenylketonurics warning under 21 CFR 172.804.
explanation: Synthetic peptide sweetener classified as Group 2B possible carcinogen by IARC in 2023. Landmark marker of industrial beverage formulations.

name: Sucralose
euDetails: Authorized high-potency sweetener under Regulation (EC) 1333/2008.
fssaiDetails: Permitted in beverages and confectionery with mandatory declaration.
fdaDetails: Approved under 21 CFR 172.831.
explanation: Chlorinated sucrose derivative ~600 times sweeter than sugar. Industrial marker of non-nutritive reformulations.

name: Mono- and Diglycerides of Fatty Acids
aliases: Mono and Diglycerides of Fatty Acids
euDetails: Authorized under Regulation (EC) 1333/2008. Re-evaluated by EFSA in 2017.
fssaiDetails: Permitted under GMP across bakery and dairy products.
fdaDetails: GRAS under 21 CFR 184.1505.
explanation: Manufactured from plant or animal fats through transesterification. Replaces whole eggs/milk to extend shelf life in ultra-processed breads and cakes.

name: Lecithin (Soy / Sunflower)
euDetails: Authorized natural phospholipid emulsifier.
fssaiDetails: Permitted under GMP in chocolate, bakery, and dairy analogs.
fdaDetails: GRAS under 21 CFR 184.1400.
explanation: Industrial emulsifier used to keep fats evenly distributed in commercial confectionery.

name: Polyglycerol Polyricinoleate (PGPR)
euDetails: Authorized in chocolate products with maximum permitted limits (5 g/kg).
fssaiDetails: Permitted in chocolate confectionery up to 0.5%.
fdaDetails: GRAS for chocolate and coatings.
explanation: Derived from castor beans. Used industrially to reduce the expensive cocoa butter content in chocolate without losing flowability.

name: TBHQ (Tert-Butylhydroquinone)
euDetails: Authorized in fats and oils up to 200 mg/kg. Under periodic scrutiny for immunotoxic and liver effects in animal studies.
fssaiDetails: Permitted in frying oils and fats up to 200 mg/kg. Standard antioxidant in Indian snacks.
fdaDetails: Permitted in fats up to 0.02% (200 ppm) of fat content under 21 CFR 172.185.
explanation: Synthetic preservative added to frying oils (especially palmolein) to prevent rancidity during extended tropical storage.
